newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia may use nukes first in self-defence.
newsitem.headline: Russia may use nukes first in self-defence.

text.p: Russia, its army demoralised by underfunding and delayed reforms, should be ready to unleash its nuclear arsenal in the event of a conventional armed attack, a Kremlin official was quoted on Tuesday as saying.

In a clear departure from Soviet-era military thinking, Ivan Rybkin, secretary of the policy-making Security Council, said a greater emphasis on the nuclear deterrent would discourage "military adventurers" bent on exploiting Russia's difficulties.
But his remarks also pinpointed Russian nervousness about NATO's plans to expand eastwards to incorporate several of Moscow's former communist allies.

"Everyone must know that in case of a direct challenge our response will be fully fledged, and we are to choose the use of means...including nuclears weapons," Rybkin told the Rossiiskaya Gazeta daily.
"Naturally we are not talking of a preventive nuclear strike but if an aggressor starts a war against us using conventional weapons, we may respond with nuclear ones," he said.

President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky later distanced the Kremlin from Rybkin's remarks, saying only the president, prime minister or foreign minister were entitled to express Russia's official position.
The world's largest nuclear arsenals established the Soviet Union as a military superpower and they remain a major diplomatic bargaining chip for Russia.

In the 1980s Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev pledged the Soviet Union would not use nuclear weapons first in any armed conflict. But Rybkin said that Russia, which inherited the bulk of the Soviet nuclear arsenals, should not follow this promise.

"We are reviewing political declarations of the past," Rybkin said. "Our people have spent decades building up a nuclear shield...And suddenly, without consulting anyone, someone says we are not going to use nuclear weapons first."
NATO never made a similar pledge because of the Warsaw Pact's superiority in conventional weaponry during the Cold War.
Rybkin said the present condition of Russia's armed forces was not as good as it was in Soviet times, adding that this justified the change of tack on the use of nuclear weapons.

"We talk about that (the use of nuclear weapons) so that military adventurers do not get tempted by the fact that at this stage our armed forces are being reformed and do not have the might they used to have," Rybkin said.

Russia's little noticed military doctrine of 1993 suggested the possibility of a nuclear response to an attack by a foreign state. But Rybkin's remarks carry renewed weight due to Moscow's fierce row with NATO over its enlargement plans and because of the parlous state of Russia's armed forces.
Russia's army, which once inspired fear in the West, was badly humiliated during an unsuccessful 21-month bid to crush rebel guerrillas in the breakaway region of Chechnya.
Last month Moscow withdrew its last troops from the region in line with a peace accord signed with the rebels.
Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said last week the armed forces faced an immediate crisis over soldiers' unpaid wages, miserable conditions, corruption and plummeting morale.
On Tuesday Rodionov repeated his warning in an interview with the Trud newspaper.

"The crisis in the Russian armed forces, the crisis in Russia's ability to defend itself, has reached its peak. We had a similar situation in the army at the end of the civil war in the 1920s," Rodionov said.
In his interview Rybkin said Russia should continue negotiating with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation to find mutually acceptable ways of solving the issue of NATO expansion.

"We are against the expansion of NATO's war machine to the east. But Russia cannot become a NATO enemy -- this would be costly and deadly...We must be able to agree and we will find an agreement," he said.
